hints: Focus on what changes with temperature and what does not. Remember that activation energy is a property of the reaction pathway.
Recall that heating gives more molecules higher energy, so the peak of the distribution must get lower, shift right and flatten out, but the total area stays the same.
Look for the curve that is broader and flatter than at T1 but still starts at the origin, with the Ea mark in exactly the same place on the energy axis.
walkthrough:
**Decide what happens to Ea**

Think of $E_a$ as the energy barrier for the reaction. It does not change when you only change temperature.

$$E_a \text{ at } T_2 = E_a \text{ at } T_1$$
So the vertical $E_a$ line must stay at the same value on the energy axis.

**Decide what happens to the distribution at higher T**

At higher temperature $T_2$, average molecular energy increases. Fewer molecules have very low energy and many more have high energy.

This means the curve still starts at 0,0, but the peak moves to the right, gets lower, and the tail to the right gets fatter. The total area under the curve stays constant because total number of molecules is unchanged.

**Match to the diagrams**

We need a flatter, broader, right-shifted curve with $E_a$ in the same horizontal position as before. That leaves only one diagram where the peak is lower and shifted right, the curve is spread out, and the fraction of molecules past $E_a$ is clearly larger.

options.A: Correct. The curve starts at the origin, the peak is lower and shifted to higher energy, and the distribution is broader, which is exactly the effect of higher temperature. $E_a$ is in the same position on the energy axis, and the area to the right of $E_a$ is larger, explaining the faster rate.
options.B: Incorrect. This curve is shifted too far to the right so that the peak (most probable energy) is now to the right of $E_a$. At a slightly higher temperature the peak should still be to the left of $E_a$, just less sharply. This overestimates the temperature effect.
options.C: Incorrect. This distribution looks essentially unchanged from $T_1$, with the same high narrow peak in the same place. A higher temperature must flatten, lower and right-shift the peak and increase the proportion of molecules with $E \ge E_a$.
options.D: Incorrect. This keeps the same high, narrow, low-energy distribution as $T_1$, so it shows no temperature effect on molecular energies. The trap is thinking $E_a$ moves left instead of the curve changing shape. In fact $E_a$ is constant and the curve must change.
